answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — an anonymous newspaper saying
answer.authorDates: First documented December 1944 · anonymous newspaper filler
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Churchill ever writing or speaking this line; the International Churchill Society searched some 2.5 million words by and about him and found nothing. The earliest documented appearance is an unsigned filler couplet in the Altoona (PA) ‘Mirror’ on 13 December 1944 — no author named.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: You make a living by what you get, but you make a life by what you give.
trail: The International Churchill Society lists it among quotes falsely attributed to Churchill ↗, noting it cannot be found in ~2.5 million words by and about him.
Etymology researcher Barry Popik ↗ dates the earliest known print to the Altoona ‘Mirror,’ 13 December 1944 — unsigned.
The rival credit to Norman MacEwen ↗ circulates widely online but rests on no cited primary source either.
source.cutTag: ↑ the 1944 original says ‘you’ and credits no one
source.excerptNote: The earliest traceable printing — an unsigned one-line filler in a 1944 small-town newspaper. It uses ‘you,’ not ‘we,’ and names no author. The polished ‘we’ wording and the Churchill byline both attach later, once the saying is already in circulation.

source.rightsNote: This is a short aphorism of unknown, anonymous origin first seen in 1944; brief sayings like it are not protected by copyright, so it is free to quote. Just don’t credit it to Churchill.

author.name: Unknown (anonymous)
author.heading: About Unknown (anonymous)
author.bio: This line has no established author. Its earliest traceable appearance is an unsigned filler couplet in the Altoona (PA) ‘Mirror’ of 13 December 1944, and it recurs through the late 1940s and 1950s in newspaper columns and church bulletins — the natural habitat of a free-floating maxim. The famous names attached to it later (Churchill, then Norman MacEwen) are decorations added after the fact, not sources.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in “Mirrorgrams,” Altoona (PA) ‘Mirror,’ 13 December 1944, p. 8, col. 2 (unsigned); citation history compiled by Barry Popik, “We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.”

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable of the “Churchillian” fakes, but the internet can’t even agree on which wrong name to use — a telltale sign of an orphan saying that later got a famous face bolted on.

items.why: The International Churchill Society ↗ files it under falsely attributed quotes: “It’s a nice quote, but definitely not Winston Churchill,” noting it turns up in none of the ~2.5 million words by and about him (it was even used in a 2005 Lockheed Martin TV ad under his name).

Quote sites pair it with “Happiness is not so much in having as sharing” and hang both on the RAF commander MacEwen, yet these listings ↗ give no book, date, or page — and the 1944 filler predates any such source.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer, per the documented citation trail ↗: an anonymous maxim in print by 1944, later dressed up in Churchill’s (or MacEwen’s) name. No evidence supports either man.

context.heading: Why the wrong name sticks
lead: The saying works as a tidy chiasmus — ‘get’ against ‘give,’ ‘living’ against ‘life’ — the kind of balanced epigram people instinctively file under a great orator. Churchill is the default magnet for any unowned line that sounds wise and vaguely British, so an anonymous 1944 newspaper filler drifted, over decades, into his mouth.

The competing MacEwen credit is instructive: when a saying is genuinely orphaned, multiple plausible-sounding attributions bloom at once, none with a page or a date behind it. That disagreement is itself the fingerprint of a misattribution.
context.pull: An orphan aphorism with a famous face bolted on — the name is decoration, not authorship.
